stem: A drawn route avoids every obstacle outline but requires a turn tighter than the robot can execute. Which conclusion follows from the lecture’s definition?

options.text: It is collision-free for the drawn point path but not feasible for the stated robot
It is feasible because its geometric curve does not cross an obstacle
It becomes feasible if it is shorter than the other routes
It is feasible if collision checking uses the full swept body, even though the turning-radius limit is still violated

stem: What can the dashed start-to-goal route around the three rectangles establish by itself?

options.text: It proves the shortest feasible route because its centerline looks shorter than other ways around the rectangles
It proves finite-body clearance because the centerline avoids the rectangles
It proves dynamic feasibility because the curve is drawn smoothly
It illustrates obstacle avoidance, but does not prove global optimality or clearance for a finite-size robot

stem: Which interpretation avoids treating the slide’s phrase “estimates its exact position” as a guarantee?

options.text: Every localization output is exact because a map gives a coordinate reference
Combining GPS and encoders makes a confidence estimate unnecessary
Agreement between fused sensors proves the pose is exact even if they share a systematic bias
Localization estimates pose from measurements; an estimate can retain uncertainty

citations.locator: Printed slide 9: Localization first bullet: estimates its exact position relative to the map.

stem: Suppose a planner recomputes a whole-map route to the destination after a road closure while the robot is moving. How should the slide’s offline/global contrast be qualified?

options.text: It is still whole-route planning in this example, although it is recomputed online
It is local planning because the computation happens online, regardless of the route’s spatial scope
It is a map update only, because marking the closure and selecting a new destination route are the same operation
It is local planning because it reacts to one changed road, even though it recomputes the complete destination route

assumptions: The planner searches the complete updated map and outputs a route to the original destination, not just an immediate steering command.

citations.locator: Printed slide 10: Global Planning bullet: complete pre-existing map and offline before movement.

stem: A free-cell centerline passes through a corridor 0.8 m wide, but the robot is 1.0 m wide and cannot rotate to reduce that width. What additional issue must the planner handle?

options.text: The robot fits because its half-width is 0.5 m, less than the corridor’s full 0.8 m width
The robot fits if each wall is inflated by 0.1 m, because 0.1 m is half the width deficit
The robot footprint does not fit; free centerline cells alone are insufficient
The centerline’s free labels prove the robot fits

assumptions: Corridor and robot widths are exact illustrative values; no deformation or alternate orientation reduces the required width.
The binary free labels describe raw point occupancy, not an already footprint-inflated configuration-space map; the body travels centered and parallel to straight corridor walls.

Printed slide 4: Core Challenge: physical size constraint.

stem: The directed map has edges A→B:3, A→C:1, C→B:7, B→E:1, B→D:5, C→D:2 and D→E:7. With additive edge costs, which A-to-E route has minimum total cost?

options.text: A→C→D→E
A→C→B→E
A→B→D→E
A→B→E

assumptions: Weights are abstract cost units because the figure does not label a physical unit. Only displayed directed edges are allowed.

stem: Why does changing a free grid from unit-cost 4-connected moves to cardinal-cost 1 and diagonal-cost √2 affect the usual BFS cost-optimality argument?

options.text: BFS still minimizes hops, but unequal step costs no longer make hop count equal total path cost
BFS minimizes geometric cost because its FIFO queue automatically prefers the cheaper of two same-depth routes
BFS must return a more expensive route on every grid containing a diagonal edge
BFS remains cost-optimal because assigning one queue entry to each move makes all move costs equal

stem: After exhaustive search of a finite represented graph, the frontier is empty and the goal was never found. What conclusion is warranted?

options.text: No route exists in that represented graph under its encoded transition rules
No physically possible route exists, even if the map omitted a valid passage
The same failure certificate would hold if the search had instead stopped at a fixed depth limit
The same failure certificate would hold if the successor generator had skipped one permitted edge

assumptions: The graph is finite and fixed; every permitted successor of each expanded vertex is considered, with correct repeated-state handling.

citations.locator: Printed slide 17: Final condition: empty frontier without finding goal means no path exists.

stem: A point robot moves in the fixed open corridor 0.3<y<0.9 m. The planning region is 0≤x≤4 m. Square grids share origin (0,0); a cell is free only if its entire closed square lies inside the open corridor. Compare cell sides 1.0 m and 0.2 m for start (0.5,0.5) m and goal (3.5,0.5) m, using 4-connected free cells. Which conclusion follows?

options.text: The coarse grid blocks the endpoints, while the fine grid represents a horizontal route; the physical corridor is unchanged
Both grids represent a route because both endpoint coordinates lie physically inside the corridor
Neither grid represents a route because the corridor width is smaller than the coarse cell side
The coarse grid represents a route but the fine grid blocks it, because finer cells create more occupied cells

assumptions: All coordinates and cell sides are supplied illustrative values, not measurements from the slide figure.
Walls occupy y≤0.3 and y≥0.9 m; any boundary contact makes a cell occupied. The robot is a point, so no additional footprint inflation is needed.
Use grid cells contained in the stated x range; there are no obstacles or forbidden transitions along the interior horizontal row.

citations.locator: Printed slide 12: Occupancy-grid binary convention and precision limitation due to grid resolution
Printed slide 15: Place vertices in cells and connect reachable neighbors

stem: In an obstacle-free square grid with cell side 0.4 m, the goal is five columns and three rows from the start. Cardinal moves cost one cell side, and diagonal moves cost sqrt(2) cell sides. What are the minimum geometric path lengths under 4-connected and 8-connected motion, respectively?
assumptions: The endpoint displacement is supplied in integer cell indices; the grid has no obstacles or boundary restrictions.
Minimize sum of geometric edge lengths, not hop count. Diagonal moves are allowed without a corner constraint because the grid is obstacle-free.

stem: Run UCS and A* from A to G on the undirected graph with edges AB=5, AC=2, BD=6, BE=3, CF=4, EF=1, ED=2, DG=6 and FG=3 km. For A*, use h(A,B,C,D,E,F,G)=(7,6,5,4,3,2,0) km. Each algorithm relaxes a vertex only for a strictly smaller g, breaks equal priorities alphabetically, and stops when G is popped. Count only non-goal expansions. Which complete record is correct?

options.text: UCS expands A,C,B,F,E,D (6); A* expands A,C,F (3); both return A→C→F→G at 9 km
UCS expands A,C,B,F (4); A* expands A,C,F (3); both return A→C→F→G at 9 km
UCS expands A,C,B,F,E,D,G (7); A* expands A,C,F,G (4); both return A→C→F→G at 9 km
UCS expands A,C,B,F,E,D (6) and returns A→C→F→E→D→G at 15 km; A* expands A,C,F (3) and returns A→C→F→G at 9 km

assumptions: Weights and heuristic labels are transcribed from the source graph; all distances use km. Both directions of each listed undirected edge are permitted.
Initialize g(A)=0 and all other g values to infinity. Use a minimum-priority frontier: g for UCS, g+h for A*. Update parent on every strictly cheaper route; do not overwrite on equal or worse routes.

Ignore stale priority entries and already-expanded vertices; the supplied heuristic is consistent on this graph, so no reopening is needed. Test the goal immediately after a valid pop, before expanding successors.
